subject: Accounting
title: Profit Margins
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Profit Margins.

hook.text: Two companies each earn $1 million. One has revenue of $5 million, the other $100 million.

buildup.text: Profit margin divides profit by revenue—showing how many cents of each dollar survive as profit.

discovery.text: Gross margin, operating margin, and net margin each tell a different part of the efficiency story.

twist.text: A 20% net margin in software is normal. A 2% margin in grocery retail is also normal.

climax.text: Falling margins over time signal pricing pressure, rising costs, or increasing competition.

punchline.text: Revenue is how much you sell. Margin is how much you keep.

quiz.question: What does profit margin measure?
options: Profit as a percentage of revenue

details.summary: Profit margins express profitability as a percentage of revenue at different levels—gross, operating, and net. This topic explains how each margin is calculated, what it measures, and how margin analysis reveals where a company's profits are generated or lost.
details.whyItMatters: Dollar profits don't tell the full story. A company earning $1 billion on $100 billion in revenue is far less efficient than one earning $1 billion on $5 billion. Margins make profitability comparable across companies of any size.
takeaways: Gross margin measures production efficiency; operating margin adds overhead efficiency; net margin captures everything
Comparing margins across periods reveals trends; comparing to peers reveals competitive position
Each margin level narrows the focus: where in the cost structure is profitability being won or lost

faq.question: What are the three main profit margins?
faq.answer: Gross margin (revenue minus COGS, divided by revenue) measures production efficiency. Operating margin (operating income divided by revenue) adds overhead costs. Net margin (net income divided by revenue) includes everything—interest, taxes, and one-time items.

faq.question: How do you use profit margins to compare companies?
faq.answer: Compare margins between competitors to see who operates more efficiently. Compare a company's margins over time to spot improving or deteriorating trends. A company with stable or expanding margins has pricing power and cost discipline; shrinking margins signal trouble.
